title: Generics

notes: Box<T> works for any type; T is chosen when you make one.
take() returns T, so the caller gets a String without casting.
Putting 42 in a Box<String> is a compile error: the point of generics.
smallest has a bound: T must be Comparable, so compareTo is allowed.
The same method works for Integers and Strings.

exercises.title: A Pair of anything
exercises.prompt: Finish generic class Pair<A, B>. first() and second() are done. Write swap() returning a new Pair<B, A> with the two swapped; <C> Pair<A, C> withSecond(C newSecond) returning a new pair with the same first and a new second; and toString() giving "(maize, 40)".

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Pair<String, Integer> p = new Pair<>("beans", 12); Pair<Integer, String> q = p.swap(); int kg = q.first() + 3; return kg + ""; }).get()
tests.name: swap keeps the types

hints: @Override public String toString() { return "(" + first + ", " + second + ")"; }

exercises.title: Best of anything
exercises.prompt: Write generic methods in Best. static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> items) and min(...) give the biggest / smallest item, or null for an empty list. static <T> T firstOr(List<T> items, T fallback) gives the first item or the fallback if empty. static <T extends Comparable<T>> boolean isSorted(List<T> items) is true if every item is <= the next (an empty or one-item list is sorted).
hints: max: if (items.isEmpty()) return null; T best = items.get(0); then compareTo in a loop.
isSorted: for i from 1, if items.get(i - 1).compareTo(items.get(i)) > 0 return false.

exercises.title: A counter for anything
exercises.prompt: Write generic class Counter<T> (use a LinkedHashMap<T, Integer> inside). add(T item) counts one more; addAll(List<T> items) adds each; count(T item) gives its count (0 if never added); distinct() gives how many different items; mostCommon() gives the item with the highest count (the one added first wins a tie), or null if nothing was added.

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Counter<String> c = new Counter<>(); c.addAll(java.util.List.of("maize", "beans", "maize")); return c.count("maize") + " " + c.count("rice") + " " + c.distinct(); }).get()
tests.name: counts

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Counter<Integer> c = new Counter<>(); c.addAll(java.util.List.of(4, 7, 7, 4, 7)); return c.mostCommon() + ""; }).get()
tests.name: mostCommon

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Counter<String> c = new Counter<>(); c.add("ORS"); c.add("ORS"); return c.count("ORS") + ""; }).get()
tests.name: add

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Counter<String> c = new Counter<>(); c.addAll(java.util.List.of("b", "a", "a", "b")); return c.mostCommon(); }).get()
tests.name: tie: first added wins
tests.hint_if_fail: Only replace the best on a strictly bigger count, and use a LinkedHashMap so order is kept.

tests.call: ((java.util.function.Supplier<String>) () -> { Counter<String> c = new Counter<>(); return c.mostCommon() + " " + c.distinct(); }).get()
tests.name: empty counter

hints: private final Map<T, Integer> counts = new LinkedHashMap<>();
mostCommon: loop over counts.entrySet(), keep the entry with the biggest value (strictly bigger).

quiz.q: What do generics mainly buy you?
choices: Type mistakes caught at compile time, and no casts
quiz.why: List<String> refuses a number when you write the code.

quiz.q: What does `<T extends Comparable<T>>` let you do inside the method?
Where does a generic method declare its type parameter?
choices: Before the return type: static <T> T first(...)

quiz.q: Is a List<Slime> a List<Enemy> (when Slime extends Enemy)?
choices: No, otherwise you could add an Archer to the slimes
quiz.why: Generic types don't follow the class hierarchy that way.
